fields.meta_title: Landscaping Landing Page for Estimate Requests | Emergent
fields.meta_description: A landscaping landing page that sends every estimate request to the person who prices it. See four examples and their rules, then build yours.
fields.h1: Build a Landscaping Landing Page That Sorts Estimate Requests
fields.hero_description: Get a landscaping landing page that sends each estimate request to the right person and keeps it in a database you own.
fields.features_heading: Six Parts That Turn a Visit Into an Estimate
fields.features_subheading: Each part below moves a landscaping landing page closer to a request someone can price. Emergent builds all six from a prompt.
fields.feature_1:
The service, picked before anything else

Open the form on the work wanted: a design project, weekly mowing, a cleanup, or grounds care. That one tap decides which questions come next and who gets the request.
fields.feature_2:
Budget ranges as buttons, not a blank box

Offer a few ranges to tap instead of a box for a number. A visitor with no figure in mind can still pick a range, and the range tells the office whether to call or to visit.
fields.feature_3:
The towns your crews reach

Name the towns or ZIP codes your crews cover, right above the form. A visitor outside them sees that before typing an address, and nobody at the office calls back to say no.
fields.feature_4:
Photos of yards you finished

Show one before-and-after pair for each service, shot on your own jobs. Put the new lawn beside the bare patch it replaced, and keep stock photos of tulips off the page.
fields.feature_5:
An alert to whoever prices the job

Write down who hears about each kind of request you take. The app Emergent builds sends that person a Slack or email alert with the visitor's address and phone number on it.
fields.feature_6:
Every request saved as a row you own

Each request is saved with its service and town in a database you own, so nothing lives only in an inbox. On paid plans Emergent exports the full code to your GitHub.

fields.tab_content_1:
Imara visits any yard with $10,000 or more to spend

Fernhollow Landscape Design opens its project form on two picks: the project type and a budget range. A request at $10,000 or more emails Imara Castellanos, the designer, to set a site visit. Smaller jobs get a phone estimate. This month 26 project requests came in: 17 reached Imara and 9 took the phone estimate.
fields.tab_content_2:
Tuesday for the north side, Friday for the south

Mossbank Lawn Care mows on fixed routes, so its page asks which side of town the yard is on and shows the mowing day right away. North side means Tuesday and South side means Friday, before anyone calls. This week 38 mowing requests came in: 23 joined Tuesday's route and 15 joined Friday's.
fields.tab_content_3:
A yard left for a year starts with a walkthrough

Birchlaw Yard Services books spring cleanups from one question: when was the yard last cleaned up? Last fall gets the standard cleanup price on the spot. Over a year ago sends Soren Abellard, the crew lead, to walk the yard first. Monday morning brought 12 cleanup requests: 7 standard and 5 walkthroughs.
fields.tab_content_4:
With year-round care, Halina writes the estimate

Stonewick Property Grounds asks commercial visitors one question: year-round care or a one-time job? Year-round requests go to Halina Grosz, the contracts estimator, and one-time jobs go to the office queue. This quarter brought 11 grounds requests: 4 to Halina and 7 to the office.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Landscaping Landing Page
fields.howto_description: Use these 7 steps to build a landscaping landing page that asks the right questions and routes each estimate request.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Give each service its own page
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Write down what each quote needs
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Name a person for each request
fields.howto_step_1_des: Point a mowing ad at a mowing page and a patio ad at a design page. A visitor who clicked for weekly mowing should not have to scroll past a design gallery to find the form.
fields.howto_step_2_des: List what you need to price each service before you write a single field. Mowing needs the side of town and the lot size, while a patio needs its rough size and what the owner plans to spend.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Put the question that decides where the request goes at the top of the form. Contact details come last, after the visitor has already told you what the job is.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Assign each kind of request to someone, such as the designer for large projects and the office for small ones. Keep one person as the fallback for anything that matches no rule.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Pick one photo pair per service
fields.howto_step_5_des: Choose a before-and-after pair for each service from your own job folders. Shoot both from the same corner of the yard and at the same time of day.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Put the services, the questions, and the routing into one prompt. Emergent builds the page and its database from that prompt, and you change any part by prompting again.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Send one test request for each service and check that it reaches the right person. Then publish the page and move your ads over to it.

faq_plan.q: What is a landscaping landing page?
faq_plan.a: A landscaping landing page is one page built for a single job: getting a yard owner to ask for an estimate. It shows yards the crew has finished and ends in a short form that asks what the yard needs and where it is.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a landscaping landing page?
faq_plan.a: Describe the page to Emergent's AI landing page builder: the services you sell, the question that sorts each request, and who prices each kind of job. From that prompt Emergent builds the form and the database behind it. Send a test request for each service, change anything by prompting again, then publish.

faq_plan.q: Which question should open the form on a landscaping landing page?
faq_plan.a: Open with the service the visitor wants, as one tap on a short list. That answer decides what the form asks next: a side of town for mowing, a budget range for a design project. Leave the name and phone number for the end.

faq_plan.q: Should mowing and design projects get separate landscaping landing pages?
faq_plan.a: Yes, if you sell both. Price mowing from the route and the lot, and book a site visit before you quote a design project. Separate pages let each ad land on the form for its own job. The same split works on a pest control landing page, where an inspection and a treatment are different requests.

faq_plan.q: Can a landscaping landing page show a price before anyone visits the yard?
faq_plan.a: Yes, for work you price the same way every time, such as weekly mowing by lot size or a standard spring cleanup. Put that price next to the button. Anything that depends on what the crew finds gets a line saying it is priced after a walkthrough.

faq_plan.q: What photos belong on a landscaping landing page?
faq_plan.a: Use before-and-after pairs from your own jobs, one pair per service you sell. Shoot both photos from the same spot so the visitor sees only the change. Leave stock garden photos off the page and show yards your own crew worked on.

faq_plan.q: How do I keep out-of-area requests off a landscaping landing page?
faq_plan.a: List the towns or ZIP codes you serve above the form, and ask for the ZIP code before anything else. A visitor outside the list sees a short note instead of the full form. Service calls raise the same problem, and the hvac landing page example writes its area rule the same way.

faq_plan.q: How does a landscaping landing page send each request to the right person?
faq_plan.a: It routes on an answer the form already collects, such as the service, the budget range, or how long the yard has gone untended. Write each rule in plain words, like design projects at $10,000 or more to the designer. The app Emergent builds sends Slack, email, or in-app alerts to whoever each rule names.

faq_plan.q: Should a landscaping landing page ask for a budget?
faq_plan.a: Yes, offered as a short set of ranges with no open number field. Set the break between ranges at the budget where you stop quoting by phone and send someone out. Each range is saved with its request in a database you own, where you can count which ranges became jobs.

faq_plan.q: Do commercial clients need their own landscaping landing page?
faq_plan.a: Yes, if you take commercial work. Ask commercial visitors about year-round care on that page, and keep the homeowner page for single yards. Emergent builds that page from its own prompt, and its requests go to whoever writes the contracts. Hardscape builds and remodels fit better on a contractor landing page.

plan.angle: The SERP for landscaping landing page is thin (MSV 20, no Semrush variants) and its AlsoAsked set is all consumer pricing and design-trend questions: nothing shows a landscaping company what happens to an estimate request after the visitor sends it. This page shows four landscaping landing pages built around the request itself: a design-build form that sends $10,000-plus projects to the designer, a mowing page that turns a side of town into a route day, a spring cleanup page that sends long-neglected yards to a walkthrough, and a commercial page that splits year-round contracts from one-time jobs. Each tab shows the form, the routing and the numbers behind it, then the steps build the same thing. No pesticide, plant-care, licensing or pricing-benchmark claims, nothing state-specific, and no third-party facts, so the page needs no domain sources. HVAC, roofing, plumber, contractor, pest control, cleaning service, electrician and solar are siblings and stay out of the headings.
